summary:
I've been building an intranet dashboard that keeps an eye on the machines in my home lab — pop-os, host01, dev01, media01 — and doubles as a launcher for the ~29 apps running across them. It's a systemd service, not a container, which was a deliberate call: its whole job is to reach out over SSH to those boxes, and running it as a plain user process meant it could just use the SSH keys and config already sitting there instead of me copying credentials into a container.

I picked up a good lesson building it around a color palette question. I'm red-green colorblind, and the first version used the usual green/amber/red status colors — which for me is basically two shades of "same." Instead of eyeballing a fix, I ran the actual palette through a colorblindness simulation and measured the color distance between states. The numbers were stark: ok-vs-fail was nearly indistinguishable under the old scheme, and a blue/amber/crimson scheme was six times more distinguishable. I also caught two counterintuitive traps that only showed up in simulation — an "accessible" vermillion I'd picked for failure states turned out to collide with the warning color, and pink desaturates toward gray for colorblind viewers and got confused with "unknown" status, which is the opposite of what I'd have guessed. There's now a test that reruns the simulation against the live stylesheet, so a future edit can't silently reintroduce a green/red pair.

Setting up CI for that project surfaced a DNS landmine worth remembering: the internal hostname I was using for git hosting is actually a real, publicly registered domain, and only its IPv4 record was overridden to point inside my network — the IPv6 record still resolves to a public server on the internet. Any client that happens to prefer IPv6 would silently push code (and credentials) to a server I don't control. It's an easy thing to overlook because everything works fine until the day some resolver behavior changes.

Elsewhere I've been doing model-serving tuning work — benchmarking a local LLM on a shared GPU to find the right thread count and memory-mapping settings. The fun result: the "obvious" move of giving it more CPU threads (going from 6 to 12) actually made generation 31% slower and far less consistent, because the extra threads were hyperthread siblings spinning and fighting each other over the same physical cores instead of doing real work.

highlights.oneLiner: Built an intranet dashboard monitoring the home lab fleet and launching ~29 apps.
Tuned local LLM serving on a shared GPU: thread count and memory-mapping settings.
